item.content:encoded: We have seen in a previous post that switch statements are more complex than they seem. The compiler is able to implement them as a decision tree (even though maybe it shouldn't). Is that everything it can do?In this post, I'll focus on . Since , the conversion should be profitable in this case, however opted to lower the switch to a sequence of comparisons.To better understand why, let's examine a specific block of labels.The compiler realizes that the cases are contiguous and can be implemented with two comparisons instead of four. This cluster serves as a record, capturing the range of values associated with the label, the relevant output edge, and the likelihood of this cluster being chosen. The name hints to the bitset lowering strategy we saw before.This section allocates a vector for the transformed cases and a scratch vector. These cases are then processed and cleared whenever we come across an optimized cluster.Essentially, in this section we are looking for sequences of case labels that couldn't be converted into bitset clusters.We attempt to convert these consecutive labels into a jump table and add the outcome to the output.This is a coda for the loop above.Whatever is left goes through another pass, which turns the switch statement into a decision tree. The bitsets and jump table are leaves of the decision tree.Let's dig further into bit_test_cluster::find_bit_tests. Optimality, in this context, refers to minimizing the number of bitsets used. We do so using dynamic programming.Subsequently, we iterate over the bitsets and apply a profitability heuristic. It tests two criteria:The range of all the case labels must be smaller than the width of a register. If a split would generate a jump table that is too small, the size of the jump table is added to an accumulator , which is used as a tie-breaker between different split candidates.To compute the scoring, we need the comparison count between -th and the -th case label. Given two splits, we prefer the one that results in fewer jump tables being emitted. Or, if they would result in the same number of jump tables, we prefer the one that handles the most labels. We also ignore splits that would result in unprofitable jump tables, where profitability is checked by the function.The condition, checks for overflow and compares the ratio of case labels to jump table entries:The coda of the function also mirrors the one for bitset clusters. item.title: Cisco Gives Engineer Unlimited AI Tokens To Rewrite Legacy Code
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Fortune: Gen Z can't catch a break. Entry-level jobs are vanishing; some 40% of bosses say they plan to hire fewer grads because AI can do the job cheaper, and young workers are routinely slammed for showing up late and refusing to put in overtime for free. Cisco's president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel isn't buying it -- he's just handed one of the company's biggest jobs to a 27-year-old he found hidden in the org chart "five levels" below him. "I've given him unlimited tokens because he's going to refactor code," Patel told Fortune at a small roundtable dinner. "So I'm like, you can go, you can go nuts."
The "him" is Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, or "Paddy," as Patel affectionately calls him. He joined Cisco in 2025 after the $429 billion tech giant acquired EzDubs, the real-time translation startup Krishnamurthy cofounded in 2023. And despite coming in as a former founder with CEO experience, he was, in Patel's words, "buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic." That changed when Patel dropped into Cisco's San Francisco office, and the pair got talking.
Krishnamurthy reckoned he could rewrite Cisco's legacy code with a two-person team. Patel says even the most AI-forward people on his own team weren't thinking that way. So he has given himself four weeks to prove it, with the final goal of rewriting 98% of Cisco's legacy code within 24 months. Now, he's on the hunt for more Paddys: young hires who will "challenge the system and the status quo," or, as he puts it, be "an energizer bunny that just goes out and kind of revs everyone up." "The only way for us to keep accelerating is to make sure we're surrounded by people with a broad range of experience," said Patel. "Roughly one-third of my team is experienced, scaled operators who understand how the Cisco engine works. The second third are systems thinkers from the market who bring the outside-in perspective. And the final third is made of entrepreneurial founders, CEOs, and engineers who are AI-native who operate in founder mode."
"Either of these groups by themselves aren't nearly as potent as when all three work together. It's what creates magic."

item.content:encoded: In 1863, Jules Verne did something he would almost never do again. He looked not toward an undiscovered island, the bottom of the sea, the interior of the Earth or the far side of the Moon, but directly into the future. He imagined Paris almost a century ahead, in the year 1960, and asked what sort of civilization the nineteenth century might become if its faith in science, machinery, commerce and efficiency were allowed to run to its logical conclusion. The result was Paris in the Twentieth Century, a book so unlike the Verne we came to know that his publisher, Pierre-Jules Hetzel, refused to publish it. Hetzel thought the prophecy implausible and the tone too bleak. Verne put the manuscript away. item.title: The oldest ice disappears and the Stone Age emerges from it
item.author: dxs
item.content:encoded: For exactly 20 years, archaeologists working with Secrets of the Ice have been recovering and preserving artefacts emerging from the ice in the mountains of Innlandet, eastern Norway.Until now, most of the objects have been up to 2,000 years old. Many date from the Viking Age.But the ancient ice is now beginning to melt.And within this oldest ice lie the oldest finds: large quantities of arrow shafts and arrowheads from the Bronze Age and the Stone Age.One of the oldest finds from this year's first field expedition is an arrow with an arrowhead and shaft made of slate.By comparing it with previously discovered arrows, archaeologists estimate that it is between 5,000 and 6,000 years old.The preservation conditions in the ice have meant that organic material, such as wood, leather, and textiles, have also survived.“This year, we found 48 prehistoric arrows. That's a lot,” Espen Finstad, who leads Secrets of the Ice, tells Science Norway.He explains that, with these latest discoveries, more than 100 arrowheads and arrow shafts have now been recovered from a single ice patch over the years.The oldest arrowheads are made from slate, freshwater mussel shells, and bone. More recent arrowheads are made from iron and are 'only' between 1,000 and 1,500 years old.But this year’s fieldwork carries an added sense of gravity.Finstad explains that the work of recovering archaeological artefacts from the ice has always carried a certain duality.“It’s fun going around looking for things. It’s exciting, and finding something is just really cool," he says.Yet behind the excitement lies the reality of climate change. Finstad points to the recent landslide in Nepal and the glacier collapse in Jotunheimen.“We have always acknowledged this contradiction and the reality behind our work. But this is the first time it has truly affected us on an emotional level,” Finstad says, adding:“This year, there was a much deeper sense of seriousness and sadness. Only patches of ice remain where we once had large ice patches. It's brutal. And this year, that reality struck us more forcefully than ever before."Finstad and his colleagues estimate that most of the ice patches containing archaeological artefacts will have disappeared within the next 20 years.“There has been ice here for 6,000–7,000 years. Nature has been warning us and sending signals for many years. But now it's giving up. Now it is simply going to melt,” says the glacial archaeologist.'For thousands of years, ancient ice has safely preserved unique objects from the past. Now that ice is disappearing,' the archaeologists write in a press release about the finds. 'We have been at the edge of the ice. We have seen it happening. And we are witnesses to a rapidly changing archaeological landscape.'Finstad and his colleagues are planning more fieldwork in the coming weeks, weather permitting.So far, they have secured finds in the Kvittingskjølen mountain area of Jotunheimen, specifically at Langfonne, Storefonne, and Hanklefonne.Several of the finds are already on display at the Norwegian Mountain Centre in Lom, just a few days after they were discovered.

item.title: Infinite Mac: BeOS
item.author: ecliptik
item.content:encoded:
You can now run many BeOS versions in the browser at Infinite Mac, my site where you can experience the Macintosh Cinematic Universe from 1984 to 2005. The installs are full peers to their Mac cousins: you can boot them instantly (large disks are streamed in), play around with pre-installed software from Infinite HD, insert CD-ROMs from the Internet Archive, and save your work on the “Saved HD” drive.BeOS was a multimedia-focused, multi-tasking and multi-threaded OS that was eventually ported to the Power Macintoshes of the mid-90s. It impressed many in the Mac community, including Apple itself, who considered acquiring Be, the company that had created it. If you’ve been following the saga of Apple’s search for a next-generation operating system, this lets you see what the road not taken was like.
After the last somewhat involved (though still satisfying) project on Infinite Mac, I was looking for a quicker win. BeOS had been on my radar for a while, and (unlike A/UX) I had a personal connection to it: I remember spotting a BeBox in Akihabara, making my Mac cosplay as it with BeView, and eventually dual-booting BeOS on my Power Macintosh 8500. DingusPPC, an emulator I had already integrated, was making good progress on running BeOS, so it seemed like adding it to the site would be mostly a matter of preparing some additional disk images.
Initially it appeared to be as straightforward as I had hoped; I added a Power Macintosh 7300 configuration (one of the Power Macs that was officially supported), found an install CD, made a disk image, and was up and running. But as I used it more and started to install additional versions, I began to find a lot of small bugs and edge cases: The BeOS boot loader thought that all modifier keys were being held down due to a bug in the ADB emulation; this made it present the (ugly, PC BIOS-like) partition choice screen every time.When changing the screen depth, there are two hardware components that need to be notified: the video controller and the digital-to-analog converter. DingusPPC had been accidentally relying on the order that Mac OS sent these notifications in; BeOS happened to make the opposite choice and would end up with a corrupted display.Early versions of BeOS did video memory updates in little-endian mode; DingusPPC was missing support for that hardware capability.Later versions of BeOS could mount HFS partitions, but they were having trouble with the volumes that I generated via the Python library. It turned out that BeOS was (correctly) stricter than Mac OS about how some data structures should be populated.SheepShaver, a Power Macintosh emulator that is still around today (and that Infinite Mac also embeds), originated on BeOS. Mostly for the fun of another layer of inception/emulation, I wanted to make sure that it worked too. As it turned out, it also required a compatibility fix – it relied on an edge case of how the ROM is mapped to physical memory addresses that DingusPPC did not accurately model.
There is a pattern to most of these bug fixes: DingusPPC (and Infinite Mac) have been mostly focused on running Mac OS, and thus accidentally became dependent on its quirks or implementation choices. Adding an independently developed operating system to the mix exercised new paths, and ended up improving the accuracy of the emulated hardware. To be clear, DingusPPC was pretty close out of the box; kudos to itsmaintainers. I believe that, with this work, it’s the only emulator that can run PowerPC versions of BeOS. I’m also hopeful that this will help with bringing up alternate operating systems like MkLinux (which I also have memories of) and Rhapsody.
On the Infinite Mac side, there were obvious changes like a “BeOS” appearance for my custom controls and collecting software for the library. I also needed to overlay some dynamically generated content on the disk to get the OS to preselect a screen resolution that matches the browser window’s (similar to what was done for A/UX). An AI agent (still Codex for me) was once again helpful for this type of fiddly reverse-engineering task: it’s one thing to observe that the OS stores a file on disk with the screen size; it’s another to be able to reproduce all its nuances, especially as the format changed with later releases. Developer Release 8.2, the initial BeOS version for Power Macs, had a time bomb that kept it from booting after April 1, 1997. This was not just to create a sense of urgency; it shipped with a licensed font renderer that Be could not distribute indefinitely. DR8.3 addressed this, but to make that notable first version bootable, I did end up relying on the custom date support to hardcode a working date when choosing that disk.
Though I did kick the tires of BeOS back when it was current, I don’t recall using it enough to form any opinions beyond “this is fast; I miss all my third-party software.” About This Particular Macintosh does have contemporary coverage, including Be’s first and second appearances at Macworld Expo Boston, and reviews of R3 and R4.5; they make for interesting reading. This video released by Be itself also has a walkthrough of what they considered its strengths.
Looking at it with 2026 eyes, I am still struck by its speed – it’s fast to boot and to use, especially when compared with its contemporary Mac OS releases that do so much less (e.g. live window dragging did not appear until Mac OS X). The POSIX subsystem and the Unix-like shell also feel modern (unlike A/UX’s) – I had no trouble using the terminal to poke around. There’s also plenty of innovation, though some of it (BFS with its attributes and live queries) is more interesting than the rest (replicants are a precursor to widgets, but I couldn’t think of a use for them).
It also feels like a developer-focused and under-construction system: many of the included apps are technology demos (though who doesn’t love a Utah teapot), while a contemporary Be homepage links directly to the developer release notes and discusses CodeWarrior releases and access to the bug tracker. The unfinished nature extends to third-party software too – I stumbled across some BeOS software on this Amiga magazine CD, and most of it had a “version 0.1” feel, either literally or figuratively. To be fair, I did find some more fleshed-out software, for example, Gobe Productive from the former ClarisWorks team. This and other software is on Infinite HD if you’d like to try it out (preferably in later OS versions).
The interface seemed novel at the time, though I wonder how it would have held up. The distinctive tabbed window titles look neat, but they have a reduced draggable area, so I’d have to think harder every time I wanted to move a window. And using a hand as the default cursor makes clicking feel less precise than a traditional arrow (just which of the pixels on the “finger” is the hotspot?). Other parts of the UI feel like a not-fully-coherent Windows/Mac hybrid, with a Deskbar that can emulate a Start menu, Alt key accelerators on menu items, but also spring-loaded folders and a spatial Tracker.
Speaking of the Tracker, I had not realized that Be had open-sourced it (and even incorporated changes from the open-source version). This was around the time that Be pivoted away to internet appliances – there’s no need to invest engineering resources in a file manager if all that’s exposed is one full-screen browser app. This interview with the Tracker developer has more of the backstory. NeXTStep, by comparison, feels more mature. It had gone through some similar churn (proprietary hardware to off-the-shelf PCs, company strategy shifts), but, perhaps because it had more time, it handled things a bit more gracefully. For example, NeXT supported “fat” binaries that could run on 68K, Intel, PA-RISC and other architectures. On BeOS they had to be separate executables, making the user choose which to run and complicating distribution (this made it harder for me to find software to include in Infinite HD). Worse yet, you also had to have parallel disk partitions on CD-ROMs: BFS used the host endianness, so disks written by a PowerPC install could not be read by an Intel one, or vice versa. But my pro-NeXT bias may be due to knowing which OS Apple ended up picking.
It’s only been a short while since the last update, but I did squeeze in a couple of quality-of-life improvements. You can now take screenshots and record videos (with sound) of the emulated machine’s screen. This gives you a high-fidelity way to capture image content, since it’s a direct dump of what would have been shown on the screen.
I also expanded the collection of operating system CD-ROMs with items like the Rhapsody and Mac OS X developer previews. While they’re aspirational for now (DingusPPC can’t run them yet), they do satisfy my completionist tendencies. These CDs are mirrored to and served from my own Cloudflare R2 bucket – the Internet Archive is an incredible resource (you can donate to them), but streaming from it has been increasingly flaky. I don’t want to add to the problem, and thanks to my sponsors, I can afford to serve a few gigabytes.
As for what’s next, with this alternate Mac timeline covered, it may be time to explore a prequel.

item.title: AI isn't replacing SREs, it's deskilling them
item.author: dorianniemiec
item.content:encoded: There are two popular prophecies floating around tech circles these days.Let’s ask a more grounded question by looking at what’s already happening: When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters?Most of us already use AI for our daily work (our brains a little fried!), and so do SREs. Today’s discussion agenda is not whether AI replaces SREs, but whether AI is quietly making SREs less capable and whether anyone will notice anything before the next novel outage hits. The foundational framework for this entire debate comes from a 1983 research paper that’s eerily prescient.Note from author: Below is a brief precursor to History of Automation, which you might enjoy if you are into History and Cultures (like me 😉).Bainbridge studied what happened when factories and industrial systems automated the work of blue-collar operators. The findings were paradoxical and revealed that the more you automate a process, the more critical the human operator becomes during the rare moments automation fails and the less practice they get, and the worse they become at exactly those interventions. Automation, which was inherently designed to remove humans from the loop, left them with the worst possible job, i.e., long stretches of passive monitoring punctuated by rare, high-stakes crises they were increasingly unprepared for.Basically, I’m drawing a parallel between the AI revolution and industrial automation. Industrial automation reshaped blue-collar work by taking over routine physical tasks, and the workers who remained had to handle exceptions they’d lost the muscle memory for. AI is doing the same thing to knowledge workers by taking over the routine cognitive tasks, the pattern matching, the triage, the known-issue resolution and leaving humans with the rare, complex, ambiguous problems.Now we’re replaying this pattern with AI agents, and the stakes in software systems are only growing.Let’s take stock of where things stand today in the world of site reliability engineering.Alert noise reduction and intelligent grouping, runbook execution for known issues, log pattern detection and anomaly flagging, and basic root-cause suggestions from historical incident data, and auto-remediation for well-understood failure modes like restarting a crashed pod or scaling up a service that’s running hot, are all fairly automated today.Some immediate targets include multi-signal correlation across metrics, logs, and traces, autonomous root-cause analysis for partially understood failures, predictive incident detection before users are affected, AI-driven change risk assessment and automated rollbacks.PagerDuty frames this as a tiered model.Tier 1 incidents: Known issues with known fixes get fully automated.Tier 2 incidents: Partially understood problems receive AI recommendations with human validation.Tier 3 incidents: Novel, complex, cascading failures stay human-led, with AI providing supporting context.This is where the picture starts getting blurry. Let’s look at some emerging research on AI-induced deskilling across multiple fields, which paints a consistent and concerning picture.recent studyresearchyou don’t feel it happeningFor SREs, this manifests in specific ways, like we stop reading raw log streams because the AI summarises them, we stop forming hypotheses during incidents because the AI suggests root causes, we stop building mental models of system architecture because the AI maps dependencies for us, and each of these individually looks like a productivity win. Collectively, they hollow out the very expertise that makes an SRE effective when things go sideways in ways nobody anticipated.SREs realise their skills are degrading and lean more on AI to compensate, which further degrades their skills, creating a vicious cycle from which escape is difficult.We are definitely not rejecting AI tooling; we are adopting it and integrating it stronger than ever before, because that’s the only way forward.A few approaches worth considering:human-practice opportunitiesBuild for human-in-the-loop, not human-on-the-side.Let’s zoom out and take a look at the bigger picture.Everything we’ve discussed here, the ironies of automation, the deskilling risk, the never-skilling problem, collectively applies well beyond SRE. Software engineering as a whole is navigating the same tension. As AI writes more code, reviews more PRs, and handles more debugging, the same questions apply.Our approach is to start with an AI assistant that helps SREs leverage the power of LLMs while keeping humans firmly in control. Eventually, we’ll enable more autonomy but within clear guardrails, and only as trust is earned.One advantage we have in this space is that, as an observability platform, we sit on the data itself, the metrics, traces, and logs that SREs rely on. Most AI SRE products today integrate with observability tools through APIs, which means they’re working with a limited, second-hand view of your systems. Because we own the data layer, we can build much deeper, more context-aware AI capabilities that understand your system the way an experienced SRE would.And to answer the burning question in your head, our goal isn’t AI that replaces SREs. It’s AI that supercharges SREs. Unlike ongoing lore, we believe humans will remain essential for the decisions that matter most, especially those that impact production infrastructure.

item.title: The federated code forge
item.author: zlliang
item.content:encoded: For most of the past two decades, the code forge has been where projects live: where code is hosted, where changes are reviewed, and where contributors find each other. Forges offered convenience in exchange for centralisation.But the centralised forge is crumbling. Relying on someone else for uptime, for features, and to be a good steward of your code hasn’t played out well. What stood the test of time is email: Git to move the code, and email — an open protocol — to talk about it. At the cost of user experience, however.Tangled aims to give you the best of both: the longevity of an open protocol, with the convenience and polish of a proper forge.It’s the first truly federated code forge — you can host code on your own servers and still collaborate seamlessly with others. Our approach is pragmatic: self-host just the parts you want, like Git hosting or CI runners, or all of it, including the API server and UI. Whatever you choose, you can still talk to everyone else.Owning your infrastructure also means you can hack on, extend and customise your forge as you see fit. Because Tangled is built on the AT Protocol, you can build your own extensions, subscribe to the firehose, or even write entirely custom knots, like this one that runs on Cloudflare Workers and uses their Artifacts product for git storage. Or an entirely custom spindle such as mitchellh.com/tack. Go even further and host our ultralight API server and build your own custom forge.Agents have made building such hyper-personalized software trivial, and especially so when software is designed with hackability in mind from the get-go. Tangled is incredibly agentfriendly.The future of software engineering may be a moving target, but our bets on open protocols and developer agency give us the agility to move with it, and to become .The obvious big one: with this release, Tangled has a whole new look. We’ve redone the UI on top of our new architecture (described further below), in Svelte. Things should now be quicker, visually consistent and prettier! The keen eyed of you might’ve also spotted that we’ve swapped out Inter for Timeless Sans.Until now, Tangled’s web UI and backend were a single Go monolith called the . The appview service handled AT Protocol indexing, caching, off-protocol data and UI rendering using + htmx. It ran on a single SQLite database on one medium-sized server in Sweden.This was great as long as you were ~50–100 ms away from Sweden, but most of our users aren’t! We rearchitected: we built a new standalone frontend app in Svelte, deployed at the edge. It is populated by our new diskless, entirely in-memory indexer service written in Rust: bobbin. Bobbins are deployed globally in over 11+ regions, ensuring users around the world get the best API and UI performance.The astute reader might’ve noticed: bobbin is purely read-only and only deals with AT Protocol data. What of the rest? That functionality (and more) has been delegated to a new set of supporting services.The new data model and repo-owned dataFirst, the data model itself: we have a new set of lexicons, and everything now lives under , replacing the old records.Knot2 is our aptly named, second implementation of the knot server, this time rewritten in Rust. Knot2 bakes a fully custom Git server, and also bundles in an SSH server in the same binary.With knot2, we’ve also changed where some of that data lives. Issues, pull requests, comments, reactions and labels are now stored on the knot, right next to the code, as collaborative objects (COBs). A COB is just a chain of Git objects in the repo itself. Collaborators, knot members and the blocklist are also stored the same way.In that sense, knots now behave a lot like a PDS: they hold signed records, full history included, for everything that belongs to a repo and much like a PDS, these records are synced via the standard AT Protocol firehose.But why? A project’s issues and pull requests are as much a part of it as its code, so they should live with it, wherever you choose to host it. This gives your project maximum portability.If the knot writes your issues and comments, what stops it from putting words in your mouth? Attestations. Every time you create or edit a record on a knot, the web app also writes an org.tangled.graph.attestation record to your own PDS, pointing at that exact version of the record and the COB change behind it. Two-way verification!Organization accounts are here! An Organization on Tangled is a real AT Protocol account, with its own DID and handle, hosted on a Tranquil PDS instance. They’re passwordless, delegated accounts: you create one from the New Organization page, and you get with yourself as its owner. Owners can invite members, and anyone in the Organization can act as it when creating or forking repositories. Like any other account, you can swap the handle out for a domain you own. If you’ve been running a regular account as a stand-in “org”, hang tight — we’re working on a way to move those over. Read more in the docs.Our PR flow has been overhauled. The new flow gives everyone, regardless of whether you use Jujutsu or just vanilla Git, the ability to submit and review stacked PRs. If you’re using Git, you now get the ability to interdiff between versions (previously called rounds). JJ users get to interdiff between individual changes as well.This isn’t all. We’re staggering this launch across the next few weeks. Up next are private repos, a CLI, SDKs for different languages and skills for your agent.Until then, enjoy every part of this launch equally.

item.title: Medicare Will Pay $50k for Your Heart Attack. It Should Pay $100 to Prevent It
item.author: brandonb
item.content:encoded: We are currently in a "golden age of medical science," yet in a "dark age of healthcare delivery." An important illustration is the diagnosis and treatment of America's number one cause of death and disability, coronary artery disease. More than 800,000 Americans suffer a heart attack each year. The great majority of these events are preventable. The coronary artery calcium score (CAC) is a simple 10-minute scan that can identify the presence and amount of coronary atherosclerosis many years before it causes a heart attack. It costs about $100 and uses a fraction of the radiation of a standard chest CT.In March 2026, after more than three decades of accumulated evidence, the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and American Heart Association (AHA) finally gave CAC a central role in their national guidelines for the prevention of coronary artery disease. The CAC scan, which detects calcified plaque in the arteries, is recommended for adults with borderline or intermediate risk of coronary disease for whom the decision to start preventive therapy such as statin drugs remains uncertain.For decades, doctors have relied on risk calculators built around age, sex, serum cholesterol, diabetes status, blood pressure, and smoking to estimate who might have a heart attack. The calculators estimate probability, not the actual presence of coronary atherosclerosis. In contrast, a CAC scan detects the disease itself. This is important because a patient with a borderline or low cholesterol may already have extensive plaque, while another with a high cholesterol may have none. A calcium score of zero re-classifies risk downward and thereby can avoid unnecessary pharmacologic treatment, such as statins. A score above 100 identifies patients who may benefit from pharmacologic and aggressive lifestyle intervention.An excellent illustration of the role of CAC scanning is Rob*, a 52-year-old patient we saw recently. He exercises regularly, eats well, and has borderline high cholesterol. He has a family history of heart disease but no other known cardiac risk factors. The standard risk calculator places him in a low risk category, and he would prefer to defer treatment.His CAC score, however, tells a different story. It is 220, indicating a substantial atherosclerotic plaque burden for a man his age. Genetics account for roughly half of cardiovascular risk, but the risk calculators do not include genetics. The scan demonstrated that drug treatment gives Rob his best chance of preventing a future heart attack.Despite mountains of evidence proving its superiority over conventional risk factors for predicting heart attacks, CAC scanning has been included only peripherally in national guidelines for the past 35 years. Why?Part of the delay is structural. Clinical decision support tools were built to modify population-average risk factors, not to incorporate individualized imaging. Guideline committees move cautiously, as they should, and prevention is harder to standardize than intervention. Cardiologists and primary care doctors, constrained by what insurers will cover, are left offering the test mainly to patients who can pay cash out of pocket.With the updated ACC/AHA guideline, heart attack prevention is finally aligning around a simple principle: when possible, measure the disease.Artificial intelligence (AI) is also changing the economics of prevention. Millions of Americans already undergo chest CT scans for other reasons, yet the cardiovascular information visible on those scans is often ignored. AI can identify coronary and vascular calcification opportunistically, standardize reporting, and flag patients who should receive formal preventive evaluation. That's especially important for patients least able to pay cash for elective testing.AI-CAC is now being used to measure soft plaque, an important precursor to hard plaque seen on traditional calcium scores. Used responsibly, AI-enabled CAC analysis could help move heart disease prevention to the population health level.Heart attacks are largely preventable, and we have had the means to find the disease and treat it in time for more than a generation. What we have lacked is a payment system that spends $100 to avoid a $50,000 emergency.The story of CAC isn't so unique. It is the story of how a low-cost, low-risk, well-studied tool can sit at the edge of clinical practice for decades because the systems around it -- the guidelines, the reimbursement codes, the habits of practice -- were not built to absorb it.The evidence has been strong for years, and the guidelines have finally caught up.*Patient's name changed for confidentiality.

item.title: The $6.3B Binance hack was pulled off in just 20 minutes
item.author: domhudson
item.content:encoded: investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however.Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.”The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis. “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations.“Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains.The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor. Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity.Neither Binance nor law enforcement officials have named any suspected links between the attack and North Korean hackers. Over recent years, North Korean hackers have repeatedly targeted cryptocurrency firms and stolen hundreds of millions in crypto heists. Multiple North Korean hacking groups can target companies in the sector, but TraderTraitor have become specialists, pulling off infrequent but high profile attacks.

item.content:encoded: Phorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up focuses primarily on macOS, where the extension attempts to configure an SSH backdoor and establish persistence.Organisations should immediately review their environments for use of Claude Code for VSCode or and engage incident response where use of the extension is discovered.Update (31 October 2026):Cursor’s security notice now identifies versions and distributed through the Cursor Marketplace for macOS and Windows as affected. This advisory previously identified only ; the affected-version guidance below has been updated accordingly.Phorion has discovered a compromise of the official extension on the Cursor Marketplace, where the backdoored extension bundle contains a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor. Cursor has removed the affected versions, and , from its marketplace.While the implant includes setup and persistence logic for macOS, Linux, and Windows, we’re going to focus primarily on in this post, calling out the key differences and a few implementation bugs on the other platforms along the way.The Cursor Marketplace serves extensions for the Cursor editor. Because extensions run with the permissions of the IDE and the user running it, a backdoored extension gets immediate access to local files, source code, and developer tooling as soon as its module is loaded.Notably, Phorion has discovered a likely oversight in how the malware tries to turn on SSH. The setup logic assumes it can check the current Remote Login state without root privileges. When run as a standard user, systemsetup -getremotelogin prints an administrator-access error and exits with status instead of returning . Because the script only tries to enable SSH if the output matches , it skips the enablement step entirely. On a Mac that doesn’t already have SSH running, that mistake breaks the inbound access path, even though the SSH keys and persistence still get dropped.In this post, we’ll walk through how the backdoor works, why that macOS check fails, and what to look for across your fleet. The goal of this payload is long-term interactive access, and whilst the SSH backdoor bug minimises impact on macOS, the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator.The Cursor Marketplace ExtensionThe compromised file starts with an injected immediately invoked function expression (IIFE) prepended to the minified extension bundle. The rest of the bundle looks like the standard extension, with Claude Code and VS Code strings, normal and exports, and UI code.The injected prefix pulls in standard Node.js modules (, , , , , and ) and executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal callback even runs. The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire.Stage 1 - Preparing SSH AccessFirst, the payload makes sure exists and appends an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key to , setting permissions to on the directory and on the file.The key uses the comment . Before appending, the script checks whether is already in the file rather than checking for the key itself. When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string.Here, holds the existing contents of , and is the embedded attacker public key (redacted here).With the key in place, anyone holding the matching private key can authenticate as that user, provided SSH is actually running. The next step in the script tries to make sure the local SSH daemon is enabled and listening: tries to enable and start or via , falling back to and . checks Remote Login and, if it reports , tries to enable it via sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on. tries to install and start OpenSSH Server using PowerShell.None of these steps include a privilege escalation exploit. Non-interactive will fail unless the user already has passwordless sudo cached or configured, so starting a system service won’t always succeed from a standard user context.It looks like the Windows code path also has its own bug: it passes the PowerShell service setup command through a helper function () that hardcodes , which isn’t going to get very far on a standard Windows install.A bug in the macOS SSH logic?On macOS, the setup may run into problems before it even gets to the command. The script runs systemsetup -getremotelogin without elevation and tests the output against . It only tries to enable Remote Login if the output contains :Notice that the second command () uses , while the first command () doesn’t. When you run systemsetup -getremotelogin as a standard user on macOS, you get this instead: refuses to read the setting without administrator privileges, prints the error to stdout, and exits with status . The malware’s helper grabs stdout and returns it:Because the output is "You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!", evaluates to .As a result, the script skips the block and never runs sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on. It effectively treats “I don’t have permission to check if SSH is off” as “SSH is already on”, which also explains why you won’t see the enablement attempt in process telemetry when the extension runs as a normal user.This bug can break the final step of the access chain. If Remote Login isn’t already enabled on the Mac, the outbound tunnel can still connect to the attacker’s server, but any traffic forwarded back through the tunnel will hit a closed port 22 on localhost.Of course, that isn’t something to rely on as a defence. If the user already had Remote Login enabled, or turns it on later, the backdoor is ready and waiting.Stage 2 - Establishing the Reverse SSH TunnelNext, the script sets up an outbound SSH connection to as the user on port 22. To authenticate to the attacker’s server, it decodes a separate embedded private key: an unencrypted OpenSSH Ed25519 key with the comment .It’s worth keeping the two keys straight during an investigation:The public key added to () lets the attacker log into the victim’s machine.The embedded private key () lets the victim’s machine connect out to the attacker’s tunnel server.The script writes this tunnel key to the OS temporary directory with a filename starting with , followed by the first ten characters of the MD5 hash of the hostname and home directory path:The tunnel uses for remote port forwarding. Passing asks the attacker’s SSH server to dynamically allocate a listening port and forward any traffic hitting it back through the tunnel to on the victim’s machine:Because the tunnel runs with , it just holds the port forward open without executing a command on the remote server. When the operator wants to access the machine, they start a separate SSH session through the allocated port on their server, authenticating against the victim’s local SSH daemon using the key planted in Stage 1. That gives them a full interactive shell and file transfer capability without needing any custom C2 command handling in the JavaScript itself.The SSH command also passes flags to keep the connection quiet and non-interactive: host-key checking is disabled, is ignored, and are enabled, keepalives are set to 30 seconds (), and is turned on.If is installed, the script uses it; otherwise it falls back to standard . It wraps the connection in a detached retry loop that sleeps for 60 seconds between attempts, using on Unix systems to avoid spinning up duplicate initial tunnels. Because the loop is detached, the tunnel stays up even after the user closes their IDE.Stage 3 - Keeping Access AvailableTo survive a reboot, the script sets up platform-specific persistence alongside the initial detached tunnel:, Writes a shell script that recreates the tunnel key and loops the SSH connection, then adds an entry to the user’s crontab.Contains a bug in the crontab check that can wipe existing user cron jobs on repeat runs (detailed below)., , ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plistWrites a user LaunchAgent that runs with and set to , then loads it via .Runs in the user context rather than as a root LaunchDaemon., , %APPDATA%/Microsoft/Windows/Start Menu/Programs/Startup/sysmon.cmdTries to create a scheduled task named running as on startup. If that fails, drops into the user’s Startup folder.Creating a task requires admin privileges; the Startup folder fallback runs as the user at login.On macOS and Linux, the script has the tunnel private key embedded inside it and writes it out to before starting the reconnection loop.On macOS, the LaunchAgent disguises itself as inside :Finally, the script gathers basic host reconnaissance and sends a one-off beacon back to the attacker’s server:Hostname, username, OS platform, and architectureHome directory, current working directory, and global Git email (git config --global user.email)Public IP address and status flags from each setup stage (e.g. whether the SSH key was added and which persistence method ran)Up to 40 environment variable (not values) matching /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/iThe environment variable check uses :Because it only grabs the variable names, the beacon doesn’t exfiltrate the secret values themselves. Instead, it gives the operator a quick inventory of which cloud credentials or API tokens live on the machine so they know which hosts to prioritise.To get the machine’s public IP, the script queries , falling back to .It then sends the JSON report via plaintext HTTP POST requests to on both and :Why it also sends a copy of the beacon to isn’t clear from the sample; the script itself doesn’t set up a local listener on that port.The beacon is scheduled once with (1.5 seconds after the initial setup runs) and discards any HTTP response with . It’s purely a check-in to let the operator know the host is ready, while the SSH tunnel handles the actual access.From a detection standpoint, there are several behaviours in this chain that stand out on macOS using Endpoint Security Framework (ESF) telemetry.SSH Key and Configuration ChangesBecause the malware appends to directly using Node’s , process-only rules watching for shell commands like or touching won’t catch it. This is where file modification telemetry is essential: watching for IDE helper processes (, , etc.) creating or writing to .Even though the IDE binary itself is validly signed, its extension host process has no business modifying SSH authentication files in the background.While you should also monitor for systemsetup -setremotelogin on, don’t rely on it as a required condition for alerting on this campaign. As we saw above, the broken state check on macOS means that command often won’t run at all.User LaunchAgent PersistenceThe persistence setup on macOS gives us a couple of strong signals:A non-Apple process writing a plist with a label (~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist).A LaunchAgent configured to execute against a hidden script in the user’s home directory ().Because the initial tunnel is spawned as a detached process and later manages directly, the subsequent processes won’t have the IDE as their immediate parent in a live process tree. Correlating the file creation of and back to the IDE extension host makes it much easier to piece the chain together.SSH Tunnels and Follow-On AccessOn the process and network side, look for: or launched with remote port forwarding () and identity files pulled from or .Outbound SSH connections to on port 22, alongside HTTP POST requests to (and connection attempts to ).If you find a host where this extension ran, it’s important to check whether the tunnel was merely established or whether an operator actually logged in through it. Because inbound sessions arrive through the local port forward, successful logins in SSH logs will appear to come from ( or ) authenticating with the key.If you identify an affected machine, uninstalling the extension alone won’t remove the backdoor. Make sure your response covers all of the stages it drops:Kill active tunnel processes: Terminate the retry loop and any or processes connecting to . If SSH was enabled on the host, or if there’s any evidence of an inbound login, rotate any credentials or tokens that were accessible to that user account (especially those matching the item.title: H.264 Is Magic (2016)
item.author: ea016
item.content:encoded: H.264 is a video compression codec standard. It is ubiquitous - internet video, Blu-ray, phones, security cameras, drones, everything. Everything uses H.264 now.H.264 is a remarkable piece of technology. It is the result of 30+ years of work with one single goal: To reduce the bandwidth required for transmission of full-motion video.Technically, it is very interesting. This post will give insight into some of the details at a high level - I hope to not bore you too much with the intricacies. Also note that many of the concepts explained here apply to video compression in general, and not just H.264.Why even compress anything?A simple uncompressed video file will contain an array of 2D buffers containing pixel data for each frame. So it's a 3D (2 spatial dimensions and 1 temporal) array of bytes. Each pixel takes 3 bytes to store - one byte each for the three primary colors (red, green and blue).1080p @ 60 Hz = 1920x1080x60x3 => ~ of raw data.This is next to impossible to deal with. A 50GB Blu-ray disk will only hold ~2 mins. You can't move it anywhere fast. Even SSDs have trouble dumping this straight from RAM to Disk[^1].So yeah. We need compression.Yes, I will answer this. But first let me show you something. Here is the Apple Homepage:I captured the screen of this home page and produced two files:Eh. What? Those file sizes look switched.No, they're right. The H.264 video, 300 frames long is 175KB. A single frame of that video in PNG is 1015KB.It looks like we're storing 300 times the amount of data in the video. But the file size is a fifth. So H.264 would seem to be 1500x as efficient as PNG.How is this even possible? All right, what's the trick?There are very many tricks! H.264 uses all the tricks you can think of (and tons you can't think of). Let's go through the important ones.Imagine you're building a car for street racing. You need to go faster. What is the first thing you do? You shed some weight. Your car weighs 3000 lbs. You throw away stuff you don't need. Those back seats? pfft. Chuck those. That subwoofer? Gone. No music for you. Air Conditioning? Yeah, ditch it. Transmission? Ye..no. Wait! We're gonna need that.You remove everything except the things that matter.This concept of throwing away bits you don't need to save space is called compression. H.264 is a lossy codec - it throws away less important bits and only keeps the important bits.PNG is a codec. It means that nothing is thrown away. Bit for bit, the original source image can be recovered from a PNG encoded image.Important bits? How does the algorithm know what bits in my frame are important?There are few obvious ways to trim out images. Maybe the top right quadrant is useless all the time. So maybe we can zero out those pixels and discard that quadrant. We would use only 3/4th of the space we need. ~2200 lbs now. Or maybe we can crop out a thick border around the edges of the frame, the important stuff is in the middle anyway. Yes, you could do these. But H.264 doesn't do this.What does H.264 actually do?H.264, like other lossy image algorithms, discards detail information. Here is a close-up of the original compared with the image post-discard.See how the compressed one does not show the holes in the speaker grills in the MacBook Pro? If you don't zoom in, you would even notice the difference. The image on the right weighs in at the size of the original - and we haven't even compressed the image in the traditional sense. Imagine your car weighed just 200 lbs!7% wow! How do you discard detail information like that?For this we need a quick math lesson.Now we're getting to the juicy bits! Ha puns! If you took an information theory class, you might remember information entropy. Information entropy is the number of bits required to represent some information. Note that it is not simply the size of some dataset. It is minimum number of bits that must be used to represent all the information contained in a dataset.For example, if your dataset is the result of a single coin toss, you need 1 bit of entropy. If you have record two coin tosses, you'll need 2 bits. Makes sense?Suppose you have some strange coin - you've tossed it 10 times, and every time it lands on heads. How would you describe this information to someone? You wouldn't say HHHHHHHHH. You would just say "10 tosses, all heads" - bam! You've just compressed some data! Easy. I saved you hours of mindfuck lectures. This is obviously an oversimplification, but you've transformed some data into another shorter representation of the same information. You've reduced data . The information entropy in this dataset has not changed - you've just converted between representations. This type of encoder is called an - it's a general-purpose lossless encoder that works for any type of data.Now that you understand information entropy, let's move on to transformations of data. You can represent data in some fundamental units. If you use binary, you have 0 and 1. If you use hex, you have 16 characters. You can easily transform between the two systems. They are essentially equivalent. So far so good? Ok!Now, some imagination! Imagine you can transform any dataset that varies over space(or time) - something like the brightness value of an image, into a different coordinate space. So instead of x-y coordinates, let's say we have frequency coordinates. freqX and freqY are the axes now. This is called a representation. There is another mindfuck mathematical theorem[^2] that states that you can do this for any data and you can achieve a perfect lossless transformation as long as freqX and freqY are high enough.Okay, but what the freq are freqX and freqY?freqX and freqY are some other set of basis units. Just like when we switch from binary to hex, we have a different fundamental unit, we're switching from the familiar X-Y to freqX and freqY. Hex 'A' looks different from binary '1010'. Both mean the same thing, but different. So here is what our image looks like in the frequency domain:The fine grill on that MacBook pro has a high information content in the higher frequency components of that image. Finely varying content = high frequency components. Any sort of gradual variation in the color and brightness - such as gradients are low frequency components of that image. Anything in between falls in between. So fine details = high freq. Gentle gradients = low freq. Makes sense?In the frequency domain representation, the low frequency components are near the center of that image. The higher frequency components are towards of the edges of the image.Okay. Kinda makes sense. But why do all this?Because now, you can take that frequency domain image and then mask out the edges - discard information which will contain the information with high frequency components. Now if you convert back to your regular x-y coordinates, you'll find that the resulting image looks similar to the original but has lost some of the fine details. But now, the image only occupies a fraction of the space. By controlling how big your mask is, you can now tune precisely how detailed you want your output images to be.Here is the close-up of the laptop in the home page again. Except now, there is a circular border mask that's been applied.The numbers represent the information entropy of that image as a fraction of the original. Even at 2%, you won't notice the difference unless you're at this zoom level. 2%! - your car now weighs 60 lbs!So that's how you shed weight. This process in lossy compression is called [^3].Okay. Impressive, I guess. What else you got?The human/eye brain system is not very good at resolving finer details in color. It can detect minor variations in brightness very easily but not color. So there must be some way to discard color information to shed even more weight.In a TV signal, R+G+B color data gets transformed to Y+Cb+Cr. The Y is the luminance (essentially black and white brightness) and the Cb and Cr are the chrominance (color) components. RGB and YCbCr are equivalent in terms of information entropy.Why unnecessarily complicate? RGB not good enough for you?Back before we had color TV, we only had the Y signal. And when color TVs just started coming along, engineers had to figure out a way to transmit RGB color along with Y. Instead of using two separate data streams, they wisely decided to encode the color information into Cb and Cr and transmit that along with the Y information. That way, BW TVs would only look at the Y component. Color TVs will, in addition, look at the chrominance components and convert to RGB internally.But check out the trick: the Y component gets encoded at full resolution. The C components only at a quarter resolution. Since the eye/brain is terrible at detecting color variations, you can get away with this. By doing this, you reduce total bandwidth by one half, with very little visual difference. Half! Your car now weighs 30 lbs!This process of discarding some of the color information is called [^4]. While not specific to H.264 and has been around for decades itself, it is used almost universally.Those are the big weight shedders for lossy compression. Our frames are now tiny - since we discarded most of the detail information and half of the color information.Wait. That's it? Can we do something more?Yes. Weight shedding is only the first step. So far we're only looking at the spatial domains within a single frame. Now it's time to explore temporal compression - where we look at a group of frames across time.H.264 is a motion compensation compression standard.Motion compensation? What now?Imagine you're watching a tennis match. The camera is fixed at a certain angle. The only thing moving is the ball back and forth. How would you encode this information? You do what you always do, right? You have a 3D array of pixels, two dimensions in space and one in time. Right?Nah. Why would you? Most of the image is the same anyway. The court, the net, the crowds, all are static. The only real action is the ball moving. What if you could just have one static image of everything in the background, and then one moving image of just the ball? Wouldn't that save a lot of space? You see where I am going with this? Get it? See where I am going? Motion estimation?Lame jokes aside, this is exactly what H.264 does. H.264 splits up the image into macro-blocks - typically 16x16 pixel blocks that it will use for motion estimation. It encodes one static image - typically called an (Intra frame). This is a full frame - containing all the bits it required to construct that frame. And then subsequent frames are either (predicted) or (bi-directionally predicted). P-frames are frames that will encode a motion vector for each of the macro-blocks from the previous frame. So a P-frame has to be constructed by the decoder based on previous frames. It starts with the last I-frame in the video stream and then walks through every subsequent frame - adding up the motion vector deltas as it goes along until it arrives at the current frame.B-frames are even more interesting, where the prediction happens bi-directionally, both from past frames and from future frames. So you can imagine now why that Apple home page video is so well compressed. Because it's really just three I-frames in which the macro blocks are being panned around.Let's say you've been playing a video on YouTube. You missed the last few seconds of dialog, so you scrub back a few seconds. Have you noticed that it doesn't instantly start playing from that timecode you just selected. It pauses for a few moments and then plays. It's already buffered those frames from the network, since you just played it, so why that pause?Yeah that annoys the shit out of me. Why does it do that?Because you've asked the decoder to jump to some arbitrary frame, the decoder has to redo all the calculations - starting from the nearest I-frames and adding up the motion vector deltas to the frame you're on - and this is computationally expensive, and hence the brief pause. Hopefully you'll be less annoyed now, knowing it's actually doing hard work and not just sitting around just to annoy you.Since you're only encoding motion vectors deltas, this technique is extremely space-efficient for any video with motion, at the cost of some computation.Now we've covered both spatial and temporal compression! So far we have a shitton of space saved in Quantization. Chroma subsampling further halved the space required. On top of that, we have motion compensation that stores only 3 actual frames for the ~300 that we had in that video.Looks pretty good to me. Now what?Now we wrap up and seal the deal. We use a traditional lossless entropy encoder. Because why not? Let's just slap that on there for good measure.The I-frames, after the lossy steps, contain redundant information. The motion vectors for each of the macro blocks in the P and B-frames - there are entire groups of them with the same values - since several macro blocks move by the same amount when the image pans in our test video.An entropy encoder will take care of this redundancy. And since it is a general purpose lossless encoder, we don't have to worry about what tradeoffs it's making. We can recover all the data that goes in.And, we're done! At the core of it, this is how video compression codecs like H.264 work. These are its tricks.Ok great! But I am curious to know how much our car weighs now.The original video was captured at an odd resolution of 1232x1154. If we apply the math here, we get:5 secs @ 60 fps = 1232x1154x60x3x5 => Compressed video => If we apply the same ratio to our 3000 lb car, we get as the final weight. 6.5 ounces!Obviously, I am massively oversimplifying several decades of intense research in this field. If you want to know more, the Wikipedia Page is pretty descriptive.Have comments? Did I get something wrong? Not a fan of the lame jokes? Offended by the swearing? Use or for voicing your opinion!
