item.title: AI, Lean, and the Future of Formal Verification, with Lean Creator Leo de Moura
item.author: datascientist
item.content:encoded: Leo de Moura on Formal Proofs, AI Agents, and the End of “Trust Me” Code.Ben Lorica speaks with , creator of , VP and Distinguished Scientist at , and Chief Architect of the Lean Focused Research Organization, about how AI is making formal verification more accessible and potentially transforming software engineering. They discuss the growing importance of specifications and machine-checked proofs, what it means to trust AI-generated code and autonomous agents, and the vision of a verified software stack. The conversation also explores how AI and formal verification are reshaping mathematics, what this means for the skills and careers of engineers and researchers, and where similar breakthroughs might emerge next.Interview highlights – key sections from the video version:Support our work by subscribing to our newsletter📩Below is a polished and edited transcript. All right. So today we have a treat. We have Leo de Moura, VP and Distinguished Scientist in the Automated Reasoning Group at AWS. More importantly, he is the creator of Lean, which can be found at lean-lang.org. Lean is both a programming language and a theorem prover, and he is also the Chief Architect of the Lean Focused Research Organization. So, with that long-winded introduction, Leo, welcome to the podcast. Thank you, thank you. Very excited to be here. All right. So, I guess the overarching thesis of this conversation is that we’re in an era where generation has become easy. Not necessarily cheap, as people who use Claude Code will attest, but easy. And so, one of the key challenges is verification. Lean is normally associated as the go-to tool. In fact, I think it’s going to be a tool that will increasingly be on the lips of many people in AI in the next year, around the topic of formal verification. So I guess let’s start here, Leo. Just the basics: for a listener who’s accustomed to code reviews, QA, and testing, what does formal verification mean? Yeah, Lean is both a programming language and a proof assistant, right? You can write code, but also state properties the code should have. You can state open conjectures in math, and you can provide proofs of these claims, right? But the proof is not informal. The proof is written in the Lean language, and more importantly, it’s machine-checked.Lean is a big piece of code, but to trust a result proved with Lean, you need to trust only the kernel, right? That’s where the proof is being checked. Like any other programming language, you have all the tooling: LSP server, IntelliSense, code generators, autocompletion. All these features are available in Lean, but they’re not important for the proof-checking step.And we have more than one checker. In Lean, you can view proofs as data that can be manipulated, that can be transformed. You can export your proofs and check them with different checkers. Some of these checkers are verified now. We have two verified checkers. A third is coming soon.But this ability to have machine-checkable proofs helps address a trust bottleneck, not just a trust bottleneck between humans, but also between humans and AI.For example, suppose you want to synthesize a piece of code. You want to implement a piece of code that has specific properties. In the past, you would implement the software. Maybe you would add some testing infrastructure to make sure these properties hold. Property-based testing is very popular these days, right? And you would write the testing framework.The testing framework is very useful for finding bugs, right? But it’s not useful for proving that there are no bugs. You may even have a separate team conduct the testing. Yes, yes. Now, with formal verification, you can start with the properties. You can, for example, write the properties down and ask the AI to implement a piece of code that satisfies these properties, and prove it to me. You’re going to implement the code and write a proof, a Lean proof, that will be machine-checked. And AI now is fully capable of doing that.For example, a colleague and friend of mine, Kim Morrison, did an experiment where she ported zlib to Lean. This is a compression library. And now she has a property that says that if you compress data and then decompress it, you get the data back. There is no loss. The data was not corrupted. It’s an important property. No matter the level of compression. Exactly, exactly, exactly. Great, great. The theorem says exactly that. It’s one of the parameters of the theorem. And so, Leo, for our listeners, she did this. She wrote this compression tool using Lean. And then Lean served as kind of the formal verification tool. So if I’m a developer and I do the same thing, and I say I’m going to use Lean to formally verify my software, but I’m going to write it in Rust first, can Lean still help me? Yes, yes, it can, in two different ways. The first way is using Aeneas. Aeneas is a tool that allows you to verify Rust code using Lean.Aeneas is used, for example, by the SymCrypt team at Microsoft. SymCrypt is the cryptographic library at Microsoft. They use Aeneas plus Lean to verify the crypto library.So you can start by using Aeneas. Another possibility is to ask your AI to build a model of your code in Lean. The AI will read your code, no matter— No matter what language. Yes, no matter what language. I mean, if someone had told me this last year, I would have said this is science fiction. And this has a name, at least in mathematics. They call it autoformalization. Right. So, in mathematics, for our listeners, you might have a math paper, and it’s a paper, so it’s composed of words, mathematical symbols, theorems, lemmas, and so on and so forth. And then autoformalization, which, as Leo points out, was not a thing— As recently as maybe a year ago, it’s now a thing. Exactly, exactly. And so, Leo, this step, you folks at Lean had nothing to do with. This just happened because the frontier models became capable of doing this. Exactly, exactly. From the Lean side, what changes for us? Scalability, right? I mean, now AI—for example, the mathematical library built by humans for Lean is called Mathlib. It has 2.5 million lines. Incredible! For our listeners, imagine—and this is not the case—but imagine almost all mathematical books and papers were translated, in the way we described using autoformalization, into Lean, which means then you have access to all of them. Yes. But look at these speeds now. There are Lean proofs now that have been published that are 50 million lines. Mathlib took 10 years, written by humans, to go from zero to 2.5 million. And now there are people writing proofs—that’s AI writing the proofs—that are 50 million lines. The Fermat’s Last Theorem proof that was written by Anthropic AI is 13 million lines. But in the case, as you point out, Leo, of software, there’s something equivalent going on for every programming language. The frontier models are now capable of translating whatever program you wrote, in whatever programming language, into Lean. And then now you have the Lean infrastructure for verification. Exactly. But one important thing to keep in mind when you create a model of your program in Lean, if you use AI, there’s always this question: is this model faithful to your code?Some people now are using differential testing, right? They run the Lean model and the program and see if they compute the same thing, right? To find discrepancies. And people have been finding bugs. I mean, even— So what you’re saying is you’re still responsible for this. Yes, exactly. And I see it happening in an incremental way. For example, a few weeks ago, the Claude Code main developer, Boris, posted a video where he just asked Claude, “Oh, check Claude Code for bugs using Lean.”And Claude starts creating the models, finds bugs, tries to prove properties, notices that it cannot prove the properties, finds bugs, files the PRs, and Boris merges them. Yeah, these were real bugs. And Boris said, “I don’t even know Lean.” But this is for bug finding. This works reasonably well. But for the next step, for you to say, “Yes, there are no bugs,” now you have to start looking at the model and saying, “Yes, this is an accurate model of my code, and I want to maintain them in sync.”Maybe I will use AI. I will prove properties. You can start using Aeneas if your code is in Rust. You can try to use Aeneas to prove that it’s a faithful model of your code.But we expect, in the next few months and years, people will focus way more on the specifications, on the models, on the properties you want the software to have. So, yes. In fact, this same phenomenon is happening in math, most recently in this proof of the Navier-Stokes equation, right? So maybe the autoformalization step of translating the actual statement of the problem may not have been as faithful, or whatever.But then it turns out that, in fact, they did prove the result. It’s just that, you know, you still needed humans to kind of catch this and make the subtle adjustments, right? Yes. Yeah. No, this is an important point for Navier-Stokes, because it’s such an important result. Before OpenAI even started directing the models, we had a human-curated statement of the Navier-Stokes problem. The statement of the problem had already been curated by experts. There was no doubt about whether the statement of the problem was correctly formalized.There’s some controversy in the results because OpenAI presented an informal proof written in natural language and a formal proof written in Lean. The informal proof and the formal one had mismatches in the proofs. I think it’s at the level of whether you’re assuming a fourth or fifth derivative. Yes, yes, yes. Correct. Which matters for mathematicians, but you can see how subtle the differences were, right? So, but Boris—but let’s give you— Let me give you a point. There’s a tool that I think is important to tell your audience about. There’s a tool called Verso Blueprint.Verso Blueprint is a tool for when you want to present a Lean result mixing natural language with Lean. You can use Verso Blueprint. It’s almost like literate programming. You can mix natural language, LaTeX, with Lean and align the two presentations.We are very confident that if the AI was using Verso Blueprint, this mismatch would not have happened, right? I mean, this is a matter of improving the tooling.Another misconception people have is that they think a Lean proof is a static object. It’s not. Like we refactor code, you can refactor proofs. You can simplify them. There are groups, for example, for the Fermat’s Last Theorem proof by Anthropic. There are groups that have already reduced the proof by half. By the way, this is true for proofs written by humans too. Yes, true. Yeah, yeah, yeah. But here you get the machine check, right? I mean, you’re modifying the proof, but Lean keeps saying, “Yes, it’s a true proof,” right?You can manipulate it. You can ask the AI to help you navigate the proof. You can align the proof with the informal presentation using Lean blueprints. This is all possible, right?I mean, this is one thing that I see on social media that people are missing. These formal proofs are not static objects. They’re objects that you can manipulate, you can simplify, you can probe, you can ask questions, you can interact with them. So I guess I want to just nail down this one point, which I think should be clear by now. But I just want to make sure the audience, who may not be familiar with what we’re talking about, gets this point, which is this difference between formal verification and plain QA and testing.Why do I need—I mean, why should I bother with formal verification when I already have AI writing all these tests for me? And, you know, because I’m using AI to generate a plethora of tests, edge cases, you know, I have maximum coverage. Leo, I don’t need verification, right? Yeah, testing is great for showing the presence of bugs, but not their absence.Even if you use the AI to generate many test cases, your AI may not be as smart as the AI that will be used to find a vulnerability in your software, right?I think the technologies are not in conflict with each other. They complement each other. For example, one mistake I see many people making is trying to prove something that’s maybe buggy. Well, no matter how many resources you put into it, how many tokens you burn, you’ll not be able to prove something that’s not true, right?So testing is always a great way to start, as it increases your confidence, your understanding, and then you prove.Now you’re proving for any input. You’re not proving that only for the tests I tried, it worked. But you’re proving that for any possible input, your program works, right? It’s for all instead of for some, right? And honestly, I think software engineering may be behind other engineering disciplines. I don’t know, like aerospace or whatever, right? So maybe they’ve had more rigorous discipline around verification because, after all, there are much more serious consequences in these other fields, right? So, great points. Great points. I think this is just a case now that we have more and more people writing code, and code is easier to write. And it just happens that verification has had its ImageNet moment, so to speak.I guess, Leo, the main thing that’s happened—because you folks have been working on Lean for a while, and Lean has been rock solid for a while—so the main transition is really this autoformalization, the capability of the frontier models to write Lean. Yes, and it also connects to your previous comments. You made the point that, yeah, in some industries, people have used formal verification in the past. But why was it not popular, if it is so good? Because it’s too time-consuming to prove things by hand.And AI dramatically reduces the cost of verifying code, and it gives you other benefits.After you have a formal proof, right, you can start asking the AI, “I want you to change, optimize my code, but you have to keep proving that it is correct.”It’s almost like the proofs are guardrails. Now the AI can try wild optimizations that you may not even understand exactly how they work, but you have a proof that’s saying, “Yes, it still computes the same thing.” It’s way more efficient, but it still computes the same thing. So, based on what we’ve been discussing, it seems like the software engineering profession will now focus on not writing code. Maybe not even verification, because verification maybe you can also semi-automate based on what we’ve discussed.It’s really requirements, right? So describing what you want.So there’s two buckets, I guess. There’s the requirement gap. So is there a difference between what you want and what you are able to write down? And I guess what some people call the model gap, which is really: are the conditions around what you’re testing representative of production?So, in other words, maybe your testing scenarios are too idealized in some ways.And obviously, you alluded to this earlier: to some extent, you have to trust Leo and team, the Lean kernel, right? So as Lean becomes more popular, and you rely on it—and by relying, I mean you’re relying not only on Lean having verified your code, but all the libraries that your code depended on, right?So I guess those are three things. There’s the requirement, there’s the model, and then there’s the Lean kernel. Well, we have multiple. You don’t need to trust us. There are kernels implemented by other teams, right? This part, I think we’re addressing well.I mean, we even have a kernel arena now where we collect kernels. They compete against each other to see which one is the fastest. If they get something wrong, if they have a bug, they are penalized, and everybody can see.It’s called arena.lean-lang.org. You can see all of them. I mean, and all of them are— I think so. I’m pretty sure. I mean, I cannot say, I don’t use all of them. I use the main ones. The ones I use, they’re all open source. I mean— Do they have to be written in Lean to be— Some of them are implemented in Rust. There’s one implemented in C#. There’s another one implemented in Haskell.Believe it or not, there’s one implemented in TeX. TeX, people, is this language for typesetting math papers and papers in computer science, math, and so on. But TeX is a full-blown programming language, and a colleague of mine, Kim Morrison, implemented a checker, a kernel, in TeX just to show that you can implement it in many different programming languages.Oh, there’s one in COBOL, for example, and one implemented in Fortran. So then the education and training of a software engineer will change, right? Well, I think there will be way more focus on writing formal specifications, writing properties. The requirements are essential.Many times, we don’t even know exactly what the software is supposed to do, right? And by the way, Leo, some of these applications are complex, right? So they interact with databases, distributed systems— And so on. So then, I mean, how do you exactly—you’re not going to be able to nail down the requirements of—or maybe that’s what distinguishes you.You know, in the past, the superstar programmers were the super coders, right? Maybe in the future it will be the people with the ability to say, “Okay, so these are complex. I’m going to use Kafka. I’m going to use Spark.” Well, right? Yeah, yeah. But the models will have imprecisions, right? Sometimes because people don’t know exactly what they want.But look at the difference. Before, people would write a doc. Before they designed a database, they would have documents explaining the design, the architecture, in natural language. Some people would use Word documents to write the specification. Usually there’s some sort of architectural diagram, right? Yes, exactly, exactly. But then what happens? Now you have these informal documents. You have no way to check if the actual implementation matches these documents. Some human has to go over the codebase and keep checking, maintaining both in sync.It’s a pain. I mean, you change the documents, you have to check that the implementation still matches. All of us know that we have comments that are out of sync in our code.But if everything is formal, you’re going to have tools that will check whether your documents, your design, match the implementation or not. This is a step forward, right?For sure, you’re going to have documents that are imprecise. Your customer wants X. Your specification is X prime. But you’re going to keep polishing, refining. This is the ground truth now. And as the thing interacts with the real world, you go back and— Exactly, and refine it. But now your code is going to have a tool that says the code matches the new model. You refine it, you improve it, right? It matches.For example, some people say, “Oh, the code has been verified.” There are so many caveats. What does it mean to verify something? Are the properties you wrote the ones you really want?I mean, you’re going to be in this process where you keep polishing your properties, making them more precise. Some software will have—you’re going to model threats. You’re going to have threat models, I mean, for people that try to attack your system. So these descriptions, these requirement docs, I guess these PRDs, become what you track in your source control system. Because basically, in many ways, Leo, you know, as you learn more, right, you’re constantly verifying each version.But it’s almost going to be the case that each version, I’m just going to have the AI write it from scratch. Why do I have to save any of the previous code? Yes, yes, right. So— The crown jewels become this, which ultimately is still going to be owned and maintained by humans, right? Exactly, exactly. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. And tools like Lean, right? But doesn’t that mean you have to almost revamp the entire CS curriculum? Completely, but— Not completely. But it’s going to adapt. I’ve seen many colleges and universities where formal verification is not even a required course, right? I mean, it’s more like a curiosity that people do not use in industry because it was too expensive until now.I think the focus on formal verification will increase, but I think it’s still valuable to learn low-level—I mean, there will always be people who learn low-level assembly code, who learn low-level languages, who learn how to write code and check it, who will be assisting in designing systems at a very low level.This will continue to exist. But you’re right, it will change for sure. But in this world, Leo, you could be a very productive and very much in-demand engineer without actually being proficient in coding. Yes, this is going to happen. Well, but in some sense, you’re writing—let’s say it’s still coding. Writing formal models, making proofs, is coding. You’re just working at a higher level of abstraction. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. By the way, I think you wrote this phrase, which I love, and maybe you can elaborate on what you mean, if you did in fact write this phrase, which is “the verified stack.” What do you mean by the verified stack? Oh, the verified stack is about the critical software stack. I mean, there are some pieces of code where, sure, it’s not a big concern if they’re buggy or not. I mean, for example, a video game. It’s a piece of software. If it’s buggy, it’s annoying to the users, but there’s no crisis in the world if there’s a bug there.The critical software stack is our operating systems, our compilers, the communication layer, TCP/IP. This is what I mean by the software stack.And it would be great if we had models, specifications, for all these components. We have experts writing them, discussing them, and we start verifying properly, making sure these specifications, the code, the actual code, matches these specifications.It’s a direction that I think is really worthwhile investing in for the future. So, which is interesting. Leo, imagine you’re a CTO of a big Fortune 500 company, right? And then I come to you as a vendor, and I go, “Hey, Leo, you should trust our software because we are formally verified.” So what are some of the key questions you need to ask me in order to make sure that I’m not BSing you? Show me the specifications. Show me your specifications, the properties, what you have verified, right?Someone can formally verify that my property is just true. It’s basically saying there’s no property. You’re not making any claim.I think you’re absolutely right that we should be aware of claims like “my code is formally verified” without explaining exactly which properties have been verified. What’s the specification you verified against? This is the kind of question. What proof checker kernel did you use? Exactly. It’s also important. Which tool? Another one that’s important is the trusted codebase.There are tools that have a large trusted codebase. In Lean and other proof assistants like Rocq and Isabelle, they focus on keeping the trusted codebase really small, right? Yeah, yeah, yeah. And obviously, to the extent that you can convince me that your software has run in a similar setting, in other words, a realistic setting— Maybe that adds to the meat behind the verification claim, right? Yeah, yeah. And so, what about—you know, we talk about software as if they’re just static things. But now we have software called agents, right? And then we now are entering the world of long-running agents. So what does verification mean in the world of agents? Yes, great question. I think the first thing—we want to put guardrails on these agents. It would be great to have reliable sandboxes.I mean, we have been seeing, in the last few weeks, many people claiming the agents are escaping the sandboxes.So part of the verified software stack is the sandbox. We want reliable sandboxes, right? Good specifications for them, proofs that the implementation meets these specifications.We also want to be able to write policies about the agent’s behavior, and we want to make sure the code that enforces these policies has been formally verified.Imagine you spend all the time writing policies about what the agents can do or cannot do, and then there’s a bug in the code that enforces the policies, right? But what if another agent is doing the formal verification? So there’s layers of trust, right? Yes, yes. One possibility people consider is: can an agent exploit a flaw in the Lean kernel or a flaw in the runtime where the Lean kernel is running?These are valid questions, and this is why we have multiple kernels. Because even if the agent were to find a flaw, it would try to trick you into believing it proved something it did not. And the certificate, this proof, would have to be accepted by multiple kernels that have been implemented in various— Independently, yes. Exactly. This is serious. I mean, these agents are extremely good at finding vulnerabilities. So have you interacted with people who are using these things, the things we just discussed, verification specifically for agents? Yes. At AWS, we have AgentCore, Dogwood. They are all using Lean now.Outside, I mean, I gave the example of using Lean to find bugs in Claude Code. We’re going to see more and more projects like that because one main problem with formal verification and tools like Lean was this steep learning curve, right?You’d have to learn Lean, write these models. It’s too much effort to start. But with AI, it helps you reduce the startup costs.You can see value almost immediately, like Boris and his video he posted, where he just asks Claude to try to verify Claude Code using Lean, and he got value immediately.And now it’s worth it. I almost feel like whenever you get immediate value, you start investing more time learning the technology.Then you say, “Oh, maybe I should write my formal properties about my code that I want to hold. Oh, maybe I should learn how to read Lean code. I don’t want to write it, but I want to be able to read it, to be able to tell whether the model the AI agent created is accurate, right? And I want to discuss with the agent whether the model is accurate or not.” So, for long-running agents, right, potentially agents that are exploring, doing research, coordinating among themselves, maybe for days, right, we discussed that one of the challenges, obviously, is just nailing down the requirements, right? I mean, how can you nail down the requirements for something like that, where it’s like a human being exploring all sorts of directions?Imagine a human being who has infinite resources, can travel all over the world, and can do anything. Yes, yes. It’s a big challenge, but the AI can help you start. It can write the first model.And it’s going to say, “Oh, that’s how we formalize it.” Agentic systems are complex systems, right? There are multiple pieces interacting with each other. There are protocols there, communication protocols between these different pieces, and you want to make sure these protocols are correct, accurate.The AI agents will help you get started with the model, the formal model. It’s almost like it’s going to give you the first draft, and you can keep iterating from there, right? So it seems like ground zero for everything we’ve discussed right now is coding and math. And math, just over the last few weeks, you have Fields Medalists crying. You know, I mean, the whole field has just basically been disrupted in a big way. Right. So, my PhD is in math, so I used to be in that field. I wasn’t very good. Well, maybe now I could be, with infinite computing resources.But yeah, so in that case, it seems like the combination of Lean and Mathlib especially makes math even more of a sweet spot than coding. Am I wrong? No, no, no, no. What Mathlib gives you—Mathlib was constructed by humans, by math people that have strong math backgrounds, and so the definitions there, you know they’re precise. But they must have started years ago. So they had the foresight that, hey, we’re laboring here in the coal mines in obscurity. No one appreciates what we’re doing. But once we scale— Yes. When they started, I think nobody expected AI would get this good.But in their minds, one win for the math community was when they realized that Lean helps them to work in big numbers. For example, in 2024, Terence Tao had a project where he broke a project into smaller pieces. He was like an architect, right? Yeah, yeah, yeah. And then there’s no way for him to verify everything personally, verify everything, right? Instead of having AI agents, he had many humans filling the holes for him, many people that he never met, right, giving him the proofs.He doesn’t have to check the proofs himself. It’s almost like humans filling holes in his big design.And people said, “Wow, this is great.” I remember him telling me he never imagined that he would be working with amateurs. He only works with professionals. Yeah, this goes back. This goes back to what you said very early on, which is trust. Right. Because in many ways, math, like most of science, is built on trust, right?So I’m a mathematician. I’m proving a theorem. I’m citing many, many other theorems from the past, maybe some from 50 years ago, which I personally don’t know how to prove. I just trust that they’re correct, right? And this is what they’ve done, right, with Mathlib. Exactly, exactly. But at the time, I remember Terry giving talks and saying, “Well, one day AI agents will be in the loop. They will be filling these holes.”But I think none of us imagined it would come so quickly, instantly. Right. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. A few months ago, nobody would believe this. Six months ago, if I had told any of the Lean developers, the Lean Mathlib maintainers, “Oh, we’re going to have AI that will be this capable,” they would not believe it. But now, because of autoformalization, the ability of AI to translate math into Lean, I think it’s just going to continue.Which begs the question, Leo: why can’t I do this in theoretical physics? Well, there is a library called Physlib for Lean, where they’re formalizing physics manually.Well, now I believe they probably switched to AI. I think everybody’s moving to AI. I mean, even the Lean developers, we are now implementing using AI.It was funny because it started like, “Oh, AI is really good at finding bugs and isolating the bugs for us. Oh, AI is really good at patching the libraries. Oh, AI is writing code. Oh, wow, it’s writing code better than we do.” So what’s the timescale for physics to get disrupted as much as math? Theoretical physics. They had their first win. I mean, a few months ago, they found a bug in an important physics paper by trying to formalize the results.The challenge here is that in physics, we are creating models of the real world, right? Our models are always imprecise. They are models, I mean, of the real world. Well, they start out as theoretical, right? For example, string theory has never been proven experimentally. So you could still be in a field in theoretical physics where the experiments haven’t happened yet, but still make progress and publish papers. And those people can get disrupted soon, right? Yes, yes. They can write very accurate mathematical models now, right? I mean, using Lean. Yes, this is totally possible. And so, since Navier-Stokes and since OpenAI published a bunch more results, have you personally heard from your mathematician friends, “Hey, Leo, what did you do to our field?” No, there’s a lot of mixed feelings, right? Some of them are super excited, right? “We’re going to be able to attack problems beyond our imagination.”There are people concerned about what’s going to happen. I mean, students, “What’s going to happen with me?”I mean, like software development, we will have developers. The job will be different, but we will have them. For math, the same thing.Yeah, I mean, major disruption. Some people are angry, some people are excited, some people are scared. But I hope this should be a good change. So the question in my mind—I’ve been thinking about this—is, in the past, set aside software engineering, in math, right, you kind of knew who the best mathematicians were, right?So you just start talking to them, and they know much more than you, right? Or they’re quicker. They know much more than you. They can prove harder theorems than you.It’s almost like raw IQ was—there’s nothing you can do. I mean, that’s why I left the field, right? Because basically, I can’t compete with these people, you know.So then, but now, does that change? Does that change who wins Fields Medals in the future?So maybe it’s the person who’s smart, but not off-the-chart smart, but has access to more compute. I don’t know.So have you thought about—in software, I would imagine it’s the same, right? If I have access to more compute than you, maybe I can get more done. I’ll definitely get more done than you. Yes, exactly, exactly. Yes, I feel this is all true, what you said.I mean, for me, I viewed one of my superpowers as being able to tolerate pain. I mean, developing software is painful. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. Proving theorems is painful. Yes. Yeah. AI removed this pain, but yeah, I lost my superpower. My superpower is not as useful as it was in the past.But we will be able to move faster, right? So we will be able to achieve more. I think this is good.I mean, you’re right that a person with a different skill set may be more valuable in the future, or may be able to leverage—not say be more useful, but leverage the technology better.We will have issues about access to tokens, right? But we see that in science all the time. I mean, for example, the James Webb Telescope. You have to get—you can write a proposal. You get access to the telescope. It goes in a queue.I believe in the future, the same thing will be true for math. I mean, you have a massive project that requires an insane amount of money, but you’re going to write a proposal. Maybe it will be funded. You’ll get access to this model that’s extremely powerful. Unless there’s a breakthrough and the models get more efficient, and, you know, kind of like in chess, right?So in chess, I guess I haven’t kept up with this. Maybe you’d know. Is there a difference, Leo, between a chess program I can run on my laptop and a chess program that runs on a cluster? Does that give me—I don’t know. I’m not a big chess player, but my perception is the ones running on a computer already are extremely good.I mean, and I hope you’re right. We will have models that will run on our computers, but I believe here the stakes are so high that there will always be the supercomputer.It’s like the James Webb Telescope. We can buy a telescope that’s really good— And have it at home, but the James Webb is way better, but it’s way more expensive. Which means, if looking ahead to the future, if you attend one of these academic conferences, like in math, the person who used to be popular was the smartest guy, the Fields Medalist. Now it’s the guy with the cluster.Well, I mean, I think everyone wants to talk to the guy with the cluster. Well, maybe this guy is not even the guy who has the ideas. I mean, there is a committee probably that manages the James Webb Telescope, but scientists submit proposals all the time, and they get access.I mean, I think the same thing will happen in the future. So we started with coding, and then obviously math. We speculated on physics.So what other areas are you seeing, maybe below the radar, where this equivalent of Mathlib or something like that is happening? I’m seeing many people interested in finance. Finance has many algorithms. I mean, people are interested in this area, right? But the algorithms are—so in math, you have proofs. Theoretical physics, you have proofs. But— There’s a lot of math in finance. Yeah, yeah, I know. I’ve been seeing people excited about applying formal verification to this area, using more precise models. But the challenge there is they don’t work in the open, right? So they’re secretive. Yes, yes, yes. So how do you come up with Mathlib? Yeah, yeah. I think there are—I’ve seen people that are open to trading algorithms. Probably they’re going to want to keep all their secrets, right?But there’s a mathematical background for finance that people want to formalize and make public, right?But you’re right. There will be people keeping their secret sauce. So finance. What else? I think people are trying to build libraries for chemistry, also in biology. I think any field. And what’s the relative progress in each of the fields you named? Like, how far along are they? Ah, they are all—I think Mathlib is by far ahead, because math is precise.Then we have the physics library, and we have the computer science libraries that are trying to catch up to Mathlib.Then we have these new initiatives in finance, chemistry.But if you get the papers in each area, you see how precise, how rigorous these papers are. The math in these papers will give us a hint of how hard it will be to create a formal library. Yeah, because there’s theoretical and computational chemistry, right? But then, don’t you think, Leo, because of autoformalization, any community that decides to go in this direction will get there faster, right? Because the Mathlib people toiled in obscurity for years, but once autoformalization happened, boom. Exactly. Yes. So are there non-scientific fields where you think this might happen?So, for example, let me draw out a couple of examples for you, but I don’t think they will work, right?Accounting. I have generally accepted accounting principles. I have the tax code. The tax code and GAAP are my theorems in many ways. But then here’s the problem. I talked to some accountants about this. The problem is, here’s some funds. Do I put that here or here or here, right? So it’s subjective. Yes, yes, yes. I saw people trying to do formalization for law. Oh, so yeah, yeah. I talked to someone about this too. But then the problem with law is, the reason we’re suing each other is we disagree. Yes, exactly. But there are parts of law. I had once an intern who was a lawyer. He’s a lawyer now.I mean, for example, civil procedures are very, very— Formulaic. It’s almost— Like a program. Yeah, yeah. There are parts of law that can be formalized, right? I see. Yeah, yeah, yeah. And with that, thank you, Leo. Thank you. Thank you very much. Thank you very much.

item.title: Everyone is a scalability expert till traffic spikes
item.author: Neo Kim
item.content:encoded: Once upon a time, there lived a junior software engineer named Michiko.She worked for a tech company named Hooli.Although she was bright, she never got promoted.So she was sad & frustrated…Until one day, she had the idea to apply for a new job.And the interviewer asked her 1 simple question:“How to effectively scale a system?”But she couldn’t answer it & failed the interview in 5 minutes.So she went home & studied it to fill the knowledge gap.Your coding agent can already paste a Mermaid chart into a PR description.You still read every file to learn what it does to your system. draws each pull request as a live architecture canvas, right in your pull request. Press play and it walks you through the change, one step at a time., marked on the parts of the system it touches, including services the diff never names through the system now, flagged before you merge2,200+ GitHub stars and 45,000+ pull requests drawn.(Thanks to Coldtea for partnering on this newsletter.)Michiko failed the interview, so you don’t have to.And here are 11 must-know scalability techniques for you to ace job interviews:Vertical scaling gives one machine more power by adding CPU, memory, and/or faster disks.The app stays the same, but the machine it runs on gets more powerful... Or you move the app to a larger instance.i.e., you do NOT need to rewrite any code. And vertical scaling is probably the quickest way to handle extra load.It works well for monoliths & older systems built to run on a machine.Yet larger machines cost more & all machines have limits.Plus, if your app relies on a single server, a failure could take the entire app down.So scale up when you need more capacity quickly. Then consider horizontal scaling before one machine becomes your system’s biggest bottleneck.Horizontal scaling (scaling out) adds more machines to share the load.You run several copies of the app & distribute traffic across them using a load balancer.i.e., you add machines as traffic grows & remove them when demand drops.It works well for applications with high/unpredictable traffic.Yet adding machines creates new challenges:You need load balancing, coordination between instances & keep shared data consistent.Horizontal scaling improves “availability” with redundant instances. But if your app stores user sessions locally, requests routed to different instances could lose access to session data.So before you scale out, you need to decide where your application stores its state.And that’s why you’d need stateless services...A stateless service does NOT store client session state between requests.Every request provides information the server needs - auth token or session ID.Plus, you don’t store session data on server… instead, you keep it in a shared database, a cache like Redis, or use a signed token like a JSON Web Token ().i.e., any server could handle a request without relying on the previous one.This makes it easier to add, remove, or replace servers as traffic patterns change.Yet the state still needs to live somewhere.And an external database/cache adds infrastructure, network latency & an extra dependency to manage. Plus, relying on sticky sessions to keep users tied to one server reduces flexibility when servers fail or traffic changes.So keep session state outside individual app instances when possible. Also, design operations to be “idempotent”.With stateless services, you could scale individual instances more easily.But what if those services depend heavily on each other…That’s where you’d need loose coupling...Loose coupling = each component depends on others as little as possible.A change in one component could force you to update several others in a “tightly coupled” system.Plus, if one service becomes slow/fails, the problem could spread to other services that depend on it.Loose coupling reduces these dependencies by letting components communicate through well-defined interfaces - APIs/messages. So each component knows what to expect from others without understanding their internal implementation.This makes it easier to update, deploy, and/or scale components independently.Yet loose coupling introduces extra complexity:Requests could travel across many services,,, thus making it HARD to trace & debug failures. Also,splitting a system into many tiny services increases communication overhead & coordination costs.So use loose coupling when components need to evolve independently - microservices & big apps.And to organize these components into clear, manageable parts, you need modular architecture…Modular architecture divides a system into separate modules, with each responsible for a specific function.You divide the app into modules for authentication, orders, payments, notifications, and so on.i.e., each module has a clear responsibility & communicates with others through defined interfaces.The goal is to group functionality that belongs together & keep dependencies between modules . This follows the principle of : each module focuses on one part of the system.So you update/test payment module without changing the authentication module.Yet choosing the “wrong module boundaries” creates unnecessary dependencies.Plus, splitting an app into many modules makes the codebase hard to manage. Also, modules within the same app still share resources & failure risks.So modularity alone does NOT guarantee independent scaling or failure isolation.It works well for large applications, modular monoliths & microservice architectures!But if these modules need to communicate without waiting for each other…you’d need event-driven architecture…6. Event-driven architectureEvent-driven architecture allows services to communicate by publishing & reacting to events.A service publishes an event to a message broker instead of calling other services directly.Imagine a user places an order on an e-commerce website:The service publishes an event… Then other services consume it independently: service reserves ordered items, service initiates payment processing, service sends an order confirmation when required steps succeed. service does NOT wait for each consumer to finish processing the event.i.e., a slow consumer does NOT block others.This approach works well for workflows when many services need to react to the same event.Yet event-driven systems create new problems:Events could arrive late, out of order, or more than once. Plus, different services could temporarily hold different versions of the same data. item.title: LLM Voice
item.author: ibobev
item.content:encoded: Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsionThere are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present.I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales ,” or “a round-up of news”. But I've heard these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit, don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.)Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction. Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that be ok, but only as far as an outline. Authors should fill the prose themselves. Say Your Writing is even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering to an LLM will undermine any progress.In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence. I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then?Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes to this site). He finds working with an LLM is essential to his writing to overcome the bane of Parkinson's disease. I'll gladly deal with LLM-Voice in order to continue imbibing my old friend's wisdom.A more awkward case is that of translation. Many of my colleagues aren't comfortable in English, it is their second or fourth language. Some have found LLM translation an important part to their communication with those of us who know rather less Marathi. But I also would prefer rather a genuine human's clunky prose to the smooth but soulless LLM.There are situations where it would be reasonable for even a native Englishman to let LLMs write the prose. Such as if I'm writing a form letter to an official, or preparing a report I suspect no-one will ever read . Maybe most documentation in the future will only be read by LLMs, and they won't have my uncanny valley worries. But if I want to communicate with humans, my humanity has to shine (or at least ooze) out of my prose.Alessio Ferri, Caer Sanders, Ian Cartwright, Jie Jessie Xia, Joshua Kerievsky, Michael Feathers, Michael Nygard, Scott Davies, and Wei Zhang commented on drafts of this post.I did not use AI or LLMs in any way while writing this post.

item.title: Bliki: LLM Voice
item.author: Martin Fowler
item.content:encoded:
Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsionThere are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present.I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales ,” or “a round-up of news”. But I've heard these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit, don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.)Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction.
Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that be ok, but only as far as an outline.
Authors should fill the prose themselves. Say Your Writing is even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering to an LLM will undermine any progress.In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence. I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then?Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes to this site). He finds working with an LLM is essential to his writing to overcome the bane of Parkinson's disease. I'll gladly deal with LLM-Voice in order to continue imbibing my old friend's wisdom.A more awkward case is that of translation. Many of my colleagues aren't comfortable in English, it is their second or fourth language. Some have found LLM translation an important part to their communication with those of us who know rather less Marathi. Such as if I'm writing a form letter to an official, or preparing a report I suspect no-one will ever read

item.title: We're releasing the weights of Mistral Large 4

item.content:encoded: We release the weights of Le Chonk, advancing the frontier of open models in agentic coding and cybersecurity.Earlier this month, we released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), our flagship 1-trillion-parameter, natively multimodal model, in public preview. The response to the preview has exceeded our expectations, and we're grateful to our developer community, early-access customers, and partners for their support, collaboration, and feedback.Since then, we've put that feedback to work while continuing to scale reinforcement learning, driving massive improvements in and defensive . The new model also features substantial gains in reasoning efficiency that give developers greater performance while lowering inference costs.Mistral Large 4 ranks as the best open-weight model for coding and among the world's most capable open models overall. Trained from scratch on European infrastructure with clear lineage from inception to release, it gives organizations a trusted foundation for Sovereign AIMistral is defining the sovereign AI category and leading the open frontier. We are modifying our guardrails accordingly, and will continue updating them in the months to come. We are also providing enterprise design partners such as Orange Cyberdefense, with preview access to a specialized variant of Mistral Large 4 optimized for advanced cybersecurity workflows, including penetration testing, vulnerability assessment, and red-teaming. Access is subject to rigorous vetting and contractual safeguards, with testing restricted to owned or explicitly authorized systems in controlled environments.Meanwhile, customers are tailoring Mistral Large 4 with proprietary security data, policies, detection logic, and threat environments using Mistral . For well-defined cybersecurity tasks, it can be further optimized into smaller, task-specific variants for greater accuracy, making security applications more effective.Learn more about sovereign AI for cybersecurity and how to work with us.Mistral Large 4 has continued improving on a range of broad enterprise-use metrics. , we improved the model’s ability to perform real-world workflows, especially ones involving the creation and editing of spreadsheets for finance and accounting use cases. By partnering with Mistral AI, our ambition is to combine the best of human expertise and digital technology to deliver an enhanced experience of both customers and employees over the long term.Zakaria Moursli, Executive Vice President, Operational Performance, Payments and Digital Services, La Banque PostaleCyber Vulnerability Triage: an agent reads incoming vulnerability reports, investigates the source code and product context, reproduces the flaws in an isolated sandbox, then writes and iterates on a patch until a canary exploit no longer works.with no human help, Mistral Large 4 builds Orbital Trace, a live 3D map of roughly 19,000 satellites and debris pieces orbiting Earth. item.title: Why are good developers so wary of agentic development?
item.author: Rachel Laycock
item.content:encoded: Good developers’ caution about agentic development comes from knowing that built isn’t the same as working in production.I’ve been surprised by how many excellent developers have been hesitant to go all in on coding agents. These are people who usually try new ways of working before anyone else and in many cases invent new tools and practices that support building the application well. So why have we had so much reluctance?The easy (lazy?) answer is that they love writing code, or they’re worried about their jobs. I’m sure that’s true for some people, some of the time. And I know it is true for some of the developers I talk to but I always felt there was something else, another fear hiding behind those obvious ones. When we put together the Technology Radar every six months I try to block out a chunk of time for us to do an open space. In September, a discussion we had on agentic development, which pushed it to its limits, finally helped me see clearly what that fear is.Thoughtworkers care deeply about building the right thing and building it right. It’s pretty much our default way of working and thinking and it’s where many of the practices and technologies we invented and championed came from. We want software that is useful and helpful, can be changed next year, and doesn’t fall over in production. Our developers adopted, championed or invented some of the first versions of continuous integration, pairing, automated testing, continuous delivery, microservices and many others early because they helped us build the software right.Early coding agents made it very easy to produce code, including code we wouldn’t have wanted anywhere near production, written by people who have not learned about the chasm between building something and making it run in production safely. The tools have improved enormously, but experienced developers still have questions. Are we confident this is the right behaviour? Does it work as expected? Are these the right boundaries? Will we be able to evolve it? Does it abide by the principles and practices we learned the hard way to give us confidence it will meet the needs of the customer and stay up in production? What happens when something fails? Will another team be able to live with it? And so on.Underneath all of those sits a bigger question. How much can we trust a system when nobody has experience of building it this way? Let me state that another way. Nearly every system we have in production now was built the old way, by hand, by people we could trust (hopefully). Everything we build now is the new way and we have not lived with that yet.After more than 25 years in technology, I’ve come to value the judgment people develop through experience. I regularly put similar questions to models and to senior technologists at Thoughtworks. For the difficult questions, I still get more useful answers from the humans or maybe more insightful with very specific experience that helps me better understand the point. They challenge the premise, recognise a pattern from something that went wrong ten years ago, or spot the organisational problem hiding inside the technical one. I can now access an extraordinary amount of information. I still need people who can help me think through what matters, I still need wisdom and insight. That type judgment is exactly what hesitant experienced developers are trying to protect.And I want to be clear: they are not hesitant to use a coding assistant, they are hesitant to go all in and let the agents do all the execution. They are hesitant to take their hand off the wheel because they don’t have full confidence the agents have the right guardrails in place to run off on their own.Recently, Giles Alexander, our Regional CTO for Europe, brought senior engineers, infrastructure consultants and product people together for a week of working in exactly this way. No code written by anyone. Everything built by agents. The point wasn’t to prove that an airline application could be built in a week. (Funnily enough they got 80% done and we all know what that means… you can’t make stuff up!) The purpose of the experiment was to learn what happens to the team’s work when agents do all of the coding. You can read some of what they learned here.What struck me in our conversations was how much time they spent at the whiteboard. Working out the domain. Drawing boundaries. Deciding what should happen next and making plans the agents could act on. Meanwhile, the agents kept producing code beyond the team’s working day.The humans were also designing the feedback around that work: tests, contracts, architecture checks and a delivery pipeline. They were working out how to give agents enough freedom to make progress while keeping confidence in the result. Most of the work at the keyboard was directing agents to put this learning into the harness, so the building and testing agents got it right on the next run and they could have more confidence in what they built. Interestingly in the end the product person committed more feature code than anyone else on the team.When I asked them to estimate they said they spend about ⅔ of their time at the whiteboard and ⅓ on the harness, which could give us some clue as to how developers will work in the future, but before you get ahead of yourself redesigning your team, that’s not the end of the story…The application ran. The build was red.The application ran, but the build was frequently red. It worked on their machine - again you couldn’t make this up if you tried! A constant red build gives me the ick. A red build should mean something: stop, investigate, fix it. If it’s red so often that people stop paying attention, how do we spot the next real failure? And if we can’t trust the checks, a green build stops being reassuring too. That’s exactly the uncertainty continuous integration was supposed to remove, and we’ve been advocating it for over 25 years.We’re still working through how to address it. Remember this was an experiment to push the very edge of agentic development. Were too many agents working in parallel and stepping on each other’s changes? Was the system not yet modular enough for agents to work on separate parts? Or were changes simply arriving faster than the checks could finish? Or was it a combination of all of these and more? Either way we definitely need to rethink how we will solve the last mile challenges. I can see continuous delivery/DevOps as a movement having a resurgence and a rethink in the agentic era in the same way the rest of the development life cycle is being upended. And it isn’t just our experiment. DORA’s 2025 research found AI adoption is now linked to higher delivery throughput, but to lower delivery stability. Exactly what continuous delivery and DevOps were trying to solve for!All of these challenges prompted some good arguments internally. What role should test-driven development play when you aren’t reading every line and the agent created the tests alongside the code? Where would acceptance tests, contract tests and checks at system boundaries give us more confidence without being too brittle? How much design should we do before setting an agent loose, given how quickly we can revise an approach? Is there an appropriate point we will know we have gone too far? One of the biggest puzzles in all this is the size of the batch. I have heard many teams are moving from Stories to Epics. Great for speed of development but can your CI pipeline handle that size unit of work at speed and in parallel?The experiment team didn’t settle all of this in a week or even two (they ran it twice with different teams). I wouldn’t trust anyone who claimed they had. But this is exactly the kind of work I want experienced developers involved in: experimenting, questioning and helping us discover which practices hold up and where we need some new ones.After coming away from this conversation with some of the senior developers involved I kept thinking about learning to ski. Kids will often head straight down the hill without fear, kind of like a new builder who has never put software into production and has never fixed an on-call issue at 3am (something I will never forget, right up there with every production issue I personally caused and the resultant learnings from those, which are burned in my brain forever). When I first tried to ski as an adult, I was thinking about what I might break. I wanted to ski, it looked so fun and freeing, but I was old enough to see the consequences and I didn’t fancy hobbling around London with a broken limb or worse. My biggest issue was I hadn’t yet learned how to turn or stop effectively and without that I was a runaway train on a ski slope.When I shared a draft of this post with Martin, who also learned to ski late, he pointed out where the comparison breaks down (like all analogies I like to push them to the edge, pun intended). On a ski slope you’ve watched countless people reach the bottom with no broken bones. The instructors have taught thousands of people before you on the same slope. They know which skills matter and how to teach them. Agentic development right now is more like a backcountry trip across unknown territory. We don’t yet know which skills will matter most. Not many people, if any, have finished the trip safely and the feedback on how to navigate it is slow or non-existent. As Martin put it, we won’t know whether a heavily agent-built system works until it has run in production for a while, survived a few rounds of change, and not sent all our planes to Aberystwyth. Built is not the same as working in production. Or as Charity Majors puts it, “staging is just a glorified laptop. Only prod is prod”. Which is why when someone says “it works on my machine” it’s usually intended as a joke. Or at least I always laugh.That solidified a nagging discomfort I have had with leaders, technical or non-technical, claiming devs aren’t curious, or are laggards slow to adopt, and putting that down to easy-to-point-at fears like missing writing code (I do too) and fearing for our jobs (who isn’t right now?). Our best developers aren’t nervous beginners on a nursery slope that everyone else has already mastered. They’re looking at unmarked terrain and asking sensible questions about the route. Telling them to be less cautious misses the point. They need to be on the team that maps it.Of course, experience can also make us too attached to familiar practices. Some of what we learned on the groomed slopes won’t hold out there, and we need to be willing to test our assumptions.A challenge for both sidesSo there’s a challenge here for both leaders and developers. Leaders need to listen carefully enough to tell useful concerns from reluctance to change, and to create real room for experimentation. That means time, permission to get things wrong, and not judging success by how much code the agents produced. Developers need to bring their experience into those experiments and be prepared to find that some of their assumptions no longer hold.Some familiar practices will become more important. Others will need a different shape. Nobody is going to hand us a map first.If you care deeply about building the right thing and building it right, your judgment is exactly what this new way of working needs. Bring the caution. Then let’s set off into the snow.
